newsitem.title: NORWAY: Key Norway cabinet member quits over tax scandal.
newsitem.headline: Key Norway cabinet member quits over tax scandal.

text.p: Former Middle East mediator Terje Roed-Larsen quit the Norwegian government on Wednesday amid a scandal over alleged irregularities in a share-option deal he profited from 10 years ago.

Roed-Larsen, Minister for National Planning in the Labour minority government, caved in after a two-week media campaign accusing him of not telling the whole story about a 600,000-crown share-option profit he made while a marketing director at fisheries company Fideco AS in 1986.

"Today I have offered to step down as cabinet minister out of consideration for the government's position as well as my own situation," said Roed-Larsen, who explained the scandal had taken on proportions that hampered his job as minister.
The announcement came about an hour after a call by Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland for a quick political solution to the scandal.

Roed-Larsen, 48, quit as special United Nations envoy to the Middle East a month ago to head the newly created portfolio for national planning. It was a key ministry in Jagland's 18-member cabinet which took office in October following the resignation of veteran premier Gro Harlem Brundtland.

Roed-Larsen, praised as a hero for helping to broker the 1993 Israel-PLO peace pact, was quickly dubbed "super minister" in charge of building "The Norwegian House", or welfare state, of the next decade. He was the darling of the press until the share-option deal surfaced.

Political analysts agreed that the scandal had become a burden for Jagland. The leftist-leaning premier sharply criticised company share-options in industry a few months ago but appeared to condone Roed-Larsen's involvement in such schemes, despite the accusations of irregularities by his key minister, analysts said.

The final straw came on Tuesday night when Norwegian television suggested that Roed-Larsen altered key dates on documents covering the 1986 share deal for tax purposes. The matter is now being investigated by the economic crime squad.
Roed-Larsen welcomed the investigation, insisted he had not done anything wrong but said he could have been better at producing information on his 10-year-old business deal.
"But it is difficult when the entire press is going all out to dig up facts," he told reporters. "I did not deserve this."
Jagland, speaking at a separate news conference, said he accepted Roed-Larsen's resignation, which will formally take effect on Friday.
"He had no choice," Jagland said. "He could not do a good job as a cabinet minister with this thing hanging over him."

Jagland said he had confidence in Roed-Larsen pending completion of the legal investigation, saying: "I strongly believe in the rule of law. I regret the situation. Roed-Larsen is a great capacity but I now have to appoint a new planning minister."
He said the resignation would not affect government policy.
Jan Petersen, leader of the opposition Conservative Party, said Roed-Larsen's resignation was logical.
"Of course this is a tragedy for him, but there is the old rule that you have to tell the truth."
